Analyzing human whole blood RNA-Seq data with PLIER2

Marc Subirana-Granés and Maria Chikina

Source: vignettes/get_started.Rmd
get_started.Rmd

Introduction

The PLIER2 package provides a two-stage framework to extract interpretable latent variables from high-dimensional transcriptomic data. It combines a standard matrix decomposition (PLIERbase) with pathway-guided factor refinement (PLIERfull), enabling:

  1. Dimensionality reduction of gene expression matrices
  2. Incorporation of prior knowledge (e.g., Gene Ontology or MSigDB)
  3. Cross-validation to select robust latent variables

Workflow overview

Quick Start

We provide three self-contained examples:

  1. Data-frame example (whole blood):
    A small dataset loaded entirely into memory. Shows basic preprocessing, z-scoring, and running PLIER2 without on-disk storage.

  2. HDF5 example (Alzheimer’s brain):
    Demonstrates how to import expression from an HDF5 file, create a file-backed FBM object, and process larger datasets using the FBM interface.

  3. Table example (pancreatic islets):
    Illustrates reading a tab-delimited count file and comparing conditions via the B matrix.

Each example follows these steps:

  1. Load & preprocess data (filter by mean/variance, then z-score)
  2. Prepare pathway annotations via getGMT() and construct the prior matrix
  3. Compute SVD (in-memory or file-backed) and infer model dimension k
  4. Run PLIERbase to initialize latent variables
  5. Run PLIERfull to refine with pathway priors and obtain summary statistics

Example 1: In-memory data.frame (Whole Blood)

2. Preprocess and z-score

We first CPM-normalize the data (when needed), filter for genes with mean expression ≥ 0.5 and variance ≥ 0.1, and then apply z-score normalization.

#  CPM normalization
dataWholeBlood_cpm <- cpmPLIER2(dataWholeBlood)

# Filter and compute row statistics
prep_wb <- preprocessPLIER2(
  Y = dataWholeBlood_cpm,
  mean_cutoff = 0.5,
  var_cutoff  = 0.1
)

# Extract filtered matrix and rowStats
wb_Y_filtered <- prep_wb$Y_filtered
wb_rowStats   <- prep_wb$rowStats


# Z-score normalization
wb_Y_z <- zscorePLIER2(
  Y_filtered = wb_Y_filtered,
  rowStats    = wb_rowStats
)

3. SVD computation and SVD K estimation

Compute a robust SVD on the normalized matrix and infer the optimal number of latent variables K.

# Determine SVD k
n_genes   <- nrow(wb_Y_z)
n_samples <- ncol(wb_Y_z)
SVD_K_wd     <- min(n_genes, n_samples) - 1
message("Using SVD K = ", SVD_K_wd)
#> Using SVD K = 35

# Compute full SVD
set.seed(1)

dataWholeBlood.svd <- rsvd(dataWholeBlood, k = SVD_K_wd)

wb_svdRes <- rsvd(
  wb_Y_z,
  k = SVD_K_wd
)

4. Estimate K for PLIER

Estimate k via permutation/elbow method

PLIER_K_wb <- num.pc(data = wb_Y_z)
#> Computing SVD
message("Inferred PLIER K = ", PLIER_K_wb)
#> Inferred PLIER K = 7

5. PLIERbase initialization

First, we initialize latent variables using PLIERbase, which performs matrix factorization without priors.

wb_baseRes <- PLIERbase(
  Y      = wb_Y_z,
  k      = PLIER_K_wb,
  svdres = wb_svdRes,
  trace  = TRUE
)
#> [1] "L1 is set to 35.1850960521726"

6. Prepare pathway priors

Next, we build a prior matrix from curated gene sets and compute the Chat object for PLIERfull.

wb_gmtList <- list(
  GTEx_Tissues = getGMT("https://maayanlab.cloud/Enrichr/geneSetLibrary?mode=text&libraryName=GTEx_Tissues_V8_2023"),
  BP            = getGMT("https://maayanlab.cloud/Enrichr/geneSetLibrary?mode=text&libraryName=GO_Biological_Process_2025"),
  MSigDB        = getGMT("https://maayanlab.cloud/Enrichr/geneSetLibrary?mode=text&libraryName=MSigDB_Hallmark_2020")
)
wb_pathMat <- gmtListToSparseMat(wb_gmtList)
wb_matched <- getMatchedPathwayMat(wb_pathMat, rownames(wb_Y_z))
wb_chatObj <- getChat(wb_matched)

7. PLIERfull

Finally, we refine the base model by integrating pathway priors using PLIERfull, which applies cross-validation.


wb_fullRes <- PLIERfull(
  Y                 = wb_Y_z,
  priorMat          = as.matrix(wb_matched),
  svdres            = wb_svdRes,
  plier.base.result = wb_baseRes,
  Chat              = wb_chatObj,
  k                 = wb_k_pl,
  doCrossval        = TRUE,
  trace             = TRUE,
  max.U.updates     = 50
)

8. Display significant latent variables 

# Display significant latent variables
wb_summary_df <- as.data.frame(wb_fullRes$summary) %>%
  dplyr::filter(FDR < 0.05 & AUC > 0.7) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(FDR) %>% 
  dplyr::rename(LV='LV index') %>% 
  dplyr::mutate(LV=paste0('LV', LV)) %>% 
  dplyr::select(LV, pathway, FDR, AUC)

datatable(
  wb_summary_df,
  filter   = "top",        
  options  = list(
    pageLength = 10,       
    autoWidth  = TRUE),
  rownames = FALSE,
  class    = "stripe hover compact") %>%
  formatSignif(c("AUC", "FDR"), 3)

In whole-blood RNA-Seq, PLIER2 latent variables recapitulate heme metabolism, mitochondrial ATP synthesis coupled electron transport (GO:0042775) and oxidative phosphorylation (GO:0006119), pathways essential for oxygen delivery and energy generation in blood. Heme metabolism reflects erythroid lineage activity and hemoglobin production in red blood cell precursors, while the mitochondrial ATP synthesis and oxidative phosphorylation components capture the bioenergetic demands of leukocytes and platelets during immune activation and hemostatic processes. The “Whole Blood Male 70–79 Up” gene set captures transcriptional signatures in peripheral blood.

Example 2: File-Backed Matrix (Alzheimer’s Brain)

This example uses HDF5 data from the ARCHS4 resource (Lachmann et al., 2018; DOI: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-018-03751-6) focused on Alzheimer’s brain samples from a Neurobiology of Disease study (Hoogland et al., 2017; DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.nbd.2017.06.008). It demonstrates the on‑disk workflow with a file‑backed FBM to handle large‑scale transcriptomic datasets.

1. Cleanup old FBM files 

output_dir <- here("output", "alzFBM")
fbm_base <- file.path(output_dir, "FBMalz")
bk_paths <- paste0(fbm_base, c(".bk", ".bk_preproc.bk", ".bk_preproc_filtered.bk"))
file.remove(bk_paths[file.exists(bk_paths)])
#> [1] TRUE TRUE TRUE

Computing CPM on a File-Backed Matrix (FBM)

For file-backed matrices (FBMs), you can compute counts-per-million (CPM) in-place—without loading the entire dataset into RAM—using the cpmPLIER2FBM() function from PLIER2:

2. Load HDF5 expression 

alz_path   <- file.path(ext, 'get_started', "human_gene_v2.5_alz.h5")
h5 <- H5File$new(alz_path, mode = "r")
expr_mat <- t(h5[["data/expression"]]$read())
genes <- h5[["meta/genes/symbol"]]$read()
samples <- h5[["meta/samples/geo_accession"]]$read()
h5$close_all()
colnames(expr_mat) <- samples
rownames(expr_mat) <- genes

3. Construct file‑backed FBM 

dir.create(output_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
alzFBM <- FBM(nrow = nrow(expr_mat), ncol = ncol(expr_mat), backingfile = fbm_base)
blk <- 1000

for(i in seq_len(ceiling(nrow(expr_mat)/blk))){
  rows <- ((i-1)*blk+1):min(i*blk, nrow(expr_mat))
  alzFBM[rows, ] <- expr_mat[rows, , drop = FALSE]
}

4. CPM, preprocess and z‑score FBM 

prep_alz <- preprocessPLIER2FBM(
  fbm        = alzFBM,
  mean_cutoff= 0.5,
  var_cutoff = 0.1
)

alz_fbm_filt <- prep_alz$fbm_filtered
alz_rowStats <- prep_alz$rowStats
zscorePLIER2FBM(alz_fbm_filt, alz_rowStats)
alz_genes <- genes[prep_alz$kept_rows]

5. SVD computation and SVD K estimation 

g_fb       <- nrow(alz_fbm_filt)
samples_fb <- ncol(alz_fbm_filt)
SVD_K_alz  <- min(g_fb, samples_fb) - 1

message("Using SVD K = ", SVD_K_alz)
#> Using SVD K = 53

set.seed(1)
alz_svdRes <- big_randomSVD(alz_fbm_filt, k = SVD_K_alz)

6. Estimate K for PLIER 

PLIER_K_alz <- num.pc(list(d = alz_svdRes$d))
message("Inferred PLIER K = ", PLIER_K_alz)
#> Inferred PLIER K = 17

7. PLIERbase initialization 

alz_baseRes <- PLIERbase(
  Y      = alz_fbm_filt,
  k      = PLIER_K_alz,
  svdres = alz_svdRes,
  trace  = TRUE
)
#> [1] "L1 is set to 44.9829536996458"
#> [1] "L2 is set to 134.948861098937"
#> Progress 1 / 200 | Bdiff=1.826270, minCor=0.856822Progress 2 / 200 | Bdiff=0.038443, minCor=0.965096Progress 3 / 200 | Bdiff=0.006582, minCor=0.964510Progress 4 / 200 | Bdiff=0.002720, minCor=0.973542Progress 5 / 200 | Bdiff=0.001726, minCor=0.985099Progress 6 / 200 | Bdiff=0.001193, minCor=0.992761Progress 7 / 200 | Bdiff=0.000901, minCor=0.996114Progress 8 / 200 | Bdiff=0.000737, minCor=0.997516Progress 9 / 200 | Bdiff=0.000625, minCor=0.998218Progress 10 / 200 | Bdiff=0.000539, minCor=0.998625Progress 11 / 200 | Bdiff=0.000467, minCor=0.998893Progress 12 / 200 | Bdiff=0.000407, minCor=0.999096Progress 13 / 200 | Bdiff=0.000356, minCor=0.999256Progress 14 / 200 | Bdiff=0.000312, minCor=0.999381Progress 15 / 200 | Bdiff=0.000276, minCor=0.999484Progress 16 / 200 | Bdiff=0.000246, minCor=0.999568Progress 17 / 200 | Bdiff=0.000221, minCor=0.999636Progress 18 / 200 | Bdiff=0.000201, minCor=0.999690Progress 19 / 200 | Bdiff=0.000184, minCor=0.999734Progress 20 / 200 | Bdiff=0.148207, minCor=0.934848Progress 21 / 200 | Bdiff=0.007964, minCor=0.987206Progress 22 / 200 | Bdiff=0.003631, minCor=0.995188Progress 23 / 200 | Bdiff=0.002611, minCor=0.997771Progress 24 / 200 | Bdiff=0.002079, minCor=0.997901Progress 25 / 200 | Bdiff=0.001680, minCor=0.998049Progress 26 / 200 | Bdiff=0.001419, minCor=0.997742Progress 27 / 200 | Bdiff=0.001278, minCor=0.997647Progress 28 / 200 | Bdiff=0.001115, minCor=0.997839Progress 29 / 200 | Bdiff=0.000974, minCor=0.998061Progress 30 / 200 | Bdiff=0.000871, minCor=0.997577Progress 31 / 200 | Bdiff=0.000803, minCor=0.997071Progress 32 / 200 | Bdiff=0.000731, minCor=0.996936Progress 33 / 200 | Bdiff=0.000651, minCor=0.997612Progress 34 / 200 | Bdiff=0.000594, minCor=0.997835Progress 35 / 200 | Bdiff=0.000535, minCor=0.998174Progress 36 / 200 | Bdiff=0.000515, minCor=0.998605Progress 37 / 200 | Bdiff=0.000462, minCor=0.998919Converged at iteration= 37 | Bdiff=0.000462,  tol=0.000500

8. Prepare pathway priors 

alz_gmtList <- list(
  GTEx_Tissues = getGMT("https://maayanlab.cloud/Enrichr/geneSetLibrary?mode=text&libraryName=GTEx_Tissues_V8_2023"),
  BP            = getGMT("https://maayanlab.cloud/Enrichr/geneSetLibrary?mode=text&libraryName=GO_Biological_Process_2025"),
  MSigDB        = getGMT("https://maayanlab.cloud/Enrichr/geneSetLibrary?mode=text&libraryName=MSigDB_Hallmark_2020")
)

alz_pathMat <- gmtListToSparseMat(alz_gmtList)
alz_matched <- getMatchedPathwayMat(alz_pathMat, alz_genes)
alz_chatObj <- getChat(alz_matched)

9. PLIERfull 

alz_fullRes <- PLIERfull(
  Y                 = alz_fbm_filt,
  priorMat          = as.matrix(alz_matched),
  svdres            = alz_svdRes,
  plier.base.result = alz_baseRes,
  Chat              = alz_chatObj,
  k                 = PLIER_K_alz,
  doCrossval        = TRUE,
  trace             = TRUE,
  max.U.updates     = 50
)

For the Alzheimer’s brain dataset, the leading latent variable matches the GTEx tissue signature “Brain - Spinal Cord (Cervical C-1) Male 50-59 Up” confirming tissue specificity in neuroanatomical context. Additional enriched processes include: Potassium Ion Transmembrane Transport, which emphasizes neuronal excitability and ion homeostasis; Aerobic Electron Transport Chain, reflecting mitochondrial function and bioenergetics; Regulation of Dendrite Development, highlighting synaptic remodeling and neural connectivity; and Ubiquitin‑Dependent Proteolysis, indicating protein quality control mechanisms relevant to neurodegeneration.

Example 3: Tab-Delimited Count File (Pancreatic Islets)

In this example, we apply the in‑memory PLIER2 workflow to RNA‑Seq count data from GEO accession GSE164416 (Wigger et al. 2021; “Multi‑omics profiling of living human pancreatic islet donors reveals heterogeneous beta cell trajectories towards type 2 diabetes”, DOI: 10.1038/s42255-021-00420-9). After preprocessing the raw counts and fitting the PLIER2 model, we perform a differential analysis of latent‑variable activities to compare non‑diabetic (ND) and type 2 diabetic (T2D) samples.

1. Load count data and map gene symbols 

islet_file <- file.path(ext, 'get_started', "GSE164416_DP_htseq_counts.txt")

islet_df <- read.table(
  islet_file,
  header = TRUE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

islet_df$symbol <- mapIds(
  org.Hs.eg.db,
  keys = islet_df$ensembl,
  column = "SYMBOL",
  keytype = "ENSEMBL",
  multiVals = "first"
)

islet_df <- islet_df[!is.na(islet_df$symbol), ]

2. Aggregate counts by gene symbol 

# Sum counts per symbol
setDT(islet_df)
num_cols <- names(islet_df)[sapply(islet_df, is.numeric)]
expr <- islet_df[, lapply(.SD, sum), by = symbol, .SDcols = num_cols]
expr <- as.data.frame(expr)
rownames(expr) <- expr$symbol
expr$symbol <- NULL
expr <- as.matrix(expr)

3. CPM, preprocess and z-score 

prep_is <- preprocessPLIER2(
  Y = expr,
  mean_cutoff = 0.5,
  var_cutoff  = 0.1
)

iso_Yf   <- prep_is$Y_filtered
iso_rowS <- prep_is$rowStats
iso_Yz   <- zscorePLIER2(Y_filtered = iso_Yf, rowStats = iso_rowS)

4. SVD computation and SVD K estimation 

# Determine SVD k for islet data
n_genes_is   <- nrow(iso_Yz)
n_samples_is <- ncol(iso_Yz)
SVD_K_is     <- min(n_genes_is, n_samples_is) - 1
message("Using SVD K = ", SVD_K_is)
#> Using SVD K = 132

# Compute SVD with determined k
set.seed(1)
islet_svdRes <- rsvd(
  iso_Yz,
  k = SVD_K_is
)

5. Estimate K for PLIER 

PLIER_K_is <- num.pc(data = iso_Yz)
#> Computing SVD
message("Inferred PLIER k = ", PLIER_K_is)
#> Inferred PLIER k = 12

6. PLIERbase initialization 

islet_baseRes <- PLIERbase(
  Y      = iso_Yz,
  k      = PLIER_K_is,
  svdres = islet_svdRes,
  trace  = TRUE
)

7. Prepare pathway priors 

islet_gmtList <- list(
  GTEx_Tissues          = getGMT('https://maayanlab.cloud/Enrichr/geneSetLibrary?mode=text&libraryName=GTEx_Tissues_V8_2023'),
  Diabetes_Perturbations = getGMT('https://maayanlab.cloud/Enrichr/geneSetLibrary?mode=text&libraryName=Diabetes_Perturbations_GEO_2022'),
  MSigDB_Hallmark       = getGMT('https://maayanlab.cloud/Enrichr/geneSetLibrary?mode=text&libraryName=MSigDB_Hallmark_2020')
)

islet_pathMat <- gmtListToSparseMat(islet_gmtList)
islet_matched <- getMatchedPathwayMat(islet_pathMat, rownames(iso_Yz))
islet_chatObj <- getChat(islet_matched)

8. PLIERfull 

islet_fullRes <- PLIERfull(
  Y                 = iso_Yz,
  priorMat          = as.matrix(islet_matched),
  svdres            = islet_svdRes,
  plier.base.result = islet_baseRes,
  Chat              = islet_chatObj,
  k                 = PLIER_K_is,
  doCrossval        = TRUE,
  trace             = TRUE,
  max.U.updates     = 50
)

In pancreatic islet RNA‑Seq, PLIER2 latent variables robustly capture islet-specific endocrine and metabolic programs. The top latent variable aligns with the GTEx “Pancreas Female 30-39 Up” signature, confirming tissue specificity. Enrichment of Myc Targets V1 and TNF‑α Signaling via NF‑κB reflects proliferative and inflammatory pathways active in islets. Protein Secretion and Oxidative Phosphorylation underline secretory and mitochondrial metabolic functions. The diabetic islet gene sets (GSE41203 NonObeseDiab Islets DN, GSE94846 PAX8-Overexpression Islet Up) highlight pathological and developmental perturbations associated with diabetes.

10. Differential latent-variable expression between conditions

Rows of the B matrix correspond to LVs and columns to samples. By grouping samples by condition (ND vs T2D), we compute average LV expression per group to identify LVs that differ between healthy and diabetic islets

B_df <- as.data.frame(as.matrix(islet_fullRes$B)) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(LV = rownames(.))

islet_meta <- file.path(ext, 'get_started', "islets_metadata.csv")

iselt_metadata <- read.csv(islet_meta, header = TRUE)

sample_types <- iselt_metadata %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    id   = as.character(id),
    type = as.character(type)
  )

sample_cols  <- setdiff(colnames(B_df), "LV")
nd_cols      <- intersect(sample_cols, sample_types$id[sample_types$type == "ND"])
other_cols   <- intersect(sample_cols, sample_types$id[sample_types$type != "ND"])

if (length(nd_cols) == 0 || length(other_cols) == 0) {
  stop("No matching ND or non-ND sample columns found")
}

lv_stats_all_vs_nd <- B_df %>%
  dplyr::rowwise() %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    Mean_ND   = mean(dplyr::c_across(dplyr::all_of(nd_cols))),
    Mean_All  = mean(dplyr::c_across(dplyr::all_of(other_cols))),
    Mean_Diff = Mean_All - Mean_ND,
    P_Value   = stats::wilcox.test(
      dplyr::c_across(dplyr::all_of(nd_cols)),
      dplyr::c_across(dplyr::all_of(other_cols))
    )$p.value
  ) %>%
  dplyr::ungroup() %>%
  dplyr::mutate(FDR = stats::p.adjust(P_Value, method = "fdr")) %>%
  dplyr::select(LV, Mean_ND, Mean_All, Mean_Diff, P_Value, FDR) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(FDR)

sig_lv_all_vs_nd <- lv_stats_all_vs_nd %>%
  dplyr::filter(FDR < 0.05)

sig_pathway <- islet_summary_df %>% 
  dplyr::filter(FDR<0.05 & AUC > 0.7) %>% 
  dplyr::filter(LV %in% sig_lv_all_vs_nd$LV) %>% 
  dplyr::arrange(FDR) %>% 
  dplyr::select(LV, pathway, FDR, AUC)

datatable(
  sig_pathway,
  filter   = "top",        
  options  = list(
    pageLength = 10,       
    autoWidth  = TRUE),
  rownames = FALSE,
  class    = "stripe hover compact"
) %>%
  formatSignif(c("AUC", "FDR"), 3)

Differential latent-variable expression highlights diabetes-related inflammation and pancreatic specificity. LV8 enriched for TNF‑α signaling via NF‑κB and cytokine-response pathways, reflecting inflammatory β‑cell stress. LV3, associated with adipose and CBP‑KO islet gene sets, suggests metabolic adaptation in disease. LV2 captures changes in α‑ versus β‑cell composition. Enrichment of pancreas-specific GTEx signatures (e.g., “Pancreas Female 30–39 Up”) further confirms tissue relevance of these latent variables.
